why: SIMPLE / MEDIUM / LARGE is not a vibe: it decides whether the port runs in one batch, in slices, or as a strangler migration behind a flag, and those strategies have very different costs. The thresholds below are calibrated against the only two real subjects this plugin has: the bundled prototype (23 screens, 24 TSX files, 4,952 source lines, 58 components) and SimpMusic (1,567 files, 1,175 Kotlin, 666 engine files, 37 screens, 64 nav destinations, 11 DI modules). Nothing here was chosen to make a particular subject land in a particular tier.

SIMPLE.label: One batch, one pass
SIMPLE.meaning: Everything fits in one context: every screen can be inspected, ported and diffed in a single batch without re-reading the prototype.

MEDIUM.label: Slices, each verified
MEDIUM.meaning: Too many screens for one context, but the app's navigation and DI can absorb new screens without a migration. Port in slices of 3-8 related screens; each slice builds, tests and diffs on its own.

LARGE.label: Strangler, per-route flag
LARGE.meaning: Beyond every MEDIUM budget in at least two dimensions. Touching the navigation graph and DI container is itself a risk, and the old UI has to keep working while slices land.

rules.classifyBy: Fit the subject against the SIMPLE budget, then the MEDIUM budget, in every dimension. The first budget it fits wins. If it fits neither, it is LARGE only when at least two dimensions are over MEDIUM (`escalation`); a single over-budget dimension stays MEDIUM with a recorded note, because one metric over is usually the heuristic misreading a fixture. A dimension the subject does not report is skipped, never counted as zero.

escalation.why: One metric over budget is usually noise in the heuristic (a prototype with a big data fixture has many files but few screens). Two is a pattern.

requirements: the override records the tier chosen and a one-line reason
the assessment's own numbers stay in `.uiport/size-assessment.json` — the override does not rewrite them
the worklog states both the computed verdict and the override, so a later reader can see the disagreement
override.why: The heuristic cannot see that a 12-screen prototype is twelve variants of one list. A human can. What it must never do is silently change the numbers.

rules.prototypeAndAppAreSeparate: A prototype can be SIMPLE while the target app is LARGE. The strategy follows the *larger* of the two, because the cost is dominated by the app's constraints (navigation, DI, engine risk), not by how much UI there is to draw.

batch.why: With under six screens the overhead of slicing (state, worklogs, per-slice diffs) exceeds the risk it reduces. No flag: a single batch that fails is reverted, not toggled.

slices.sliceBy: user journey, not file adjacency: home -> album -> now playing is one slice; all settings screens are another
slices.subagents: one per slice, after the slice's screens are mapped
slices.rollback: revert the slice's commits; slices are dependency-ordered so a later slice never has to be reverted to undo an earlier one
slices.why: Each slice has to be independently shippable, or 'sliced' only means 'split into commits'.
slices.flagNote: No flag by default — slices land in dependency order and the old screen is deleted in the same slice. Add one only if the slice cannot ship behind a build.

flag.state: each route records which side renders it, so a half-ported app is never ambiguous
flag.why: The old UI has to keep working while slices land; a global build-time flag cannot express 'home is new, settings is old'.

strangler.sliceBy: dependency order: a route can only switch after everything it navigates into is switchable, or the user falls out of the new UI mid-journey
strangler.subagents: one per slice, plus one reviewer per engine touch
strangler.rollback: flip the route's flag back; the old composable is never deleted until the slice is accepted
strangler.why: Strangler means the app is always shippable. If a slice cannot be rolled back by a flag flip, it is not a strangler, it is a rewrite with extra steps.

advisory.why: Shown to the human at the gate as context for the verdict. Not part of the computation — the budgets decide the tier, these explain what the budgets cannot see.

weights.why: the unit of work and of acceptance
a deep navigation graph is where a port breaks behaviour, not pixels
engine files are the protected boundary; more of them means more decisions at the gate
every wired screen has to reach the container somehow

cannotSee.why: counted in the budgets for context fit but blind to difficulty: 20k lines of generated data is not harder to port than 2k, only harder to read
twenty variants of one list are one screen of work; only a human can see that, and only an override can record it
